title: Oxygen loss came with a 0.05 pH fall on density 26.5 on North Atlantic sections A20 and A22 in 2012-2021
abstract: We test carbon and carbonate changes on the North Atlantic density class with unresolved oxygen loss. Joint good GLODAPv2.2023 samples on A20 and A22 at 26-36 N give 2012-2021 oxygen changes of -14.4 and -18.3 umol/kg and calculated total-scale pH changes of -0.053 and -0.055 on sigma0 26.5. Flag-2 pH at 25 C gives falls of 0.054 and 0.055 on supported subsets. The calculated fall remains about 0.025-0.027 after adverse DIC and alkalinity shifts of 4 umol/kg per cruise. An oxygen-use counterfactual at carbon:oxygen = 117:170 gives 44% and 53% of the pH fall. These are chemical equivalents, not causal shares. Salt-normalized carbon rises by 29-31 umol/kg; a carbon diagnostic that removes fixed-ratio oxygen use and carbonate dissolution rises by about 16. Its direct-oxygen counterpart remains positive under the primary calibration stress, but larger carbon:oxygen ratios and some sampling choices permit zero. The remaining carbon can include anthropogenic uptake and changed source properties. The later endpoint pH rate is faster than in 1997-2012, but season and systematic errors limit that comparison. This adds a joint chemical target and a reproducible carbonate test. It does not identify the missing oxygen process, separate respiration from ventilation, or determine future loss. Code, aggregate results, figures, source hashes and clean reproduction checks are included; source records remain external.
